extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of metaphysics / systematic philosophy
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts and evaluates principles about the nature of matter, the proper form of explanation (mechanical vs dynamical), and the methodological starting-points of philosophy (self-consciousness, idea, and will). This is a chapter-length treatment intended as a systematic metaphysical argument rather than a how-to or empirical scientific guideline.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope of mechanical explanation
rubrics_metrics.description: The application of mechanical explanatory hypotheses, beyond what is demonstrably mechanical, is entirely unjustified; many phenomena (e.g., light, heat, electricity) will always admit only of a dynamical explanation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Author insists one should not extend mechanical hypotheses beyond demonstrably mechanical cases. Mechanical hypotheses are appropriate only where demonstrably mechanical; beyond that, dynamical explanations (appealing to original forces different from impact, pressure, weight, etc.) are required. The text cites Acoustics as mechanical but rejects mechanical accounts for light and heat.

rubrics_metrics.name: Light is non-mechanical
rubrics_metrics.description: Light is neither an emanation nor a vibration and is subject to no mechanical laws; it belongs to another order of things than the mechanical.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Empirical illustration: a ray of light during a storm remains undisturbed while wind moves everything else — showing light 'stands there unmoved like a ghost'. The author treats molecular/atomic constructions of light as 'a revolting absurdity' and cites Ampère's article as an example of atomistic error.

rubrics_metrics.name: Skepticism about atomism
rubrics_metrics.description: The assumption of atoms (absolute indivisible particles) is unjustified; atoms are a fixed idea of certain savants and are not compelled by understanding or experience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Arguments offered: continuity of motion need not be composed of innumerable instantaneous motions; Kant's dialectical defense of atoms is a sophism; porosity and compressibility arguments can be interpreted without positing atoms. The author criticizes atomism as transcending possibility of experience and as a consequence of shallow metaphysics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Empirical criterion for atomism (porosity/compressibility mismatch)
rubrics_metrics.description: The assumption of atoms rests upon the phenomena of differences in specific gravity and compressibility; both must co-occur in like measure for atomism to be plausible, which empirical examples contradict.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: water has lower specific gravity than metals but is almost entirely incompressible; if atomism implied fewer atoms and larger interstices for water, it should be more compressible. Thus the correlation atomism requires is absent. Further conceptual objections: even if pores existed ad infinitum, the leftover would be dense but not necessarily absolutely indivisible atoms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Matter as objective activity / causality
rubrics_metrics.description: Matter is objective activity in general — causality thought objectively and as that which fills space; matter, as such, is not an object of perception but of thought and functions as the permanent substratum produced by the forms of the intellect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguishes matter from a priori intuitions: matter can be thought away (unlike space/time) and thus contains an a posteriori element; matter enters experience only with form and quality and is the condition of external experience rather than a directly given perceptual object.

rubrics_metrics.name: Matter is the visibility of the will
rubrics_metrics.description: Matter is simply the visibility (objectivity) of the will: as thing-in-itself a thing is will, and as phenomenon it is matter; body is the objectivity/visibility of our will.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the central metaphysical identification: whatever appears as empirical matter is the will objectified under the forms of the intellect (space, time, causality). Consequences: matter for itself would be the will (incorporeal), and all empirical properties (including gravity) are manifestations of the will and therefore a posteriori.

rubrics_metrics.name: Origin of forms in matter
rubrics_metrics.description: The temporal origin of forms, shapes, or species should reasonably be sought in matter (the visibility of the will), because matter assumes form by means of the functions of the intellect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Author invokes the Schoolmen's dictum 'Materia appetit formam' and argues that the origination of species and forms is metaphysically traced to matter. Empirical considerations about propagation and the persistence of species are discussed (see generatio æquivoca discussion).

rubrics_metrics.name: Generatio æquivoca plausible at low grades
rubrics_metrics.description: Spontaneous generation (generatio æquivoca) is probable for very low grades of life (entozoa, epizoa), particularly under special pathological or environmental circumstances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Author rejects the universal-spores-in-air hypothesis as more paradoxical. Examples: pediculus arising in disease, plant growth after forest burning, vegetation on newly formed coral islands, putrefaction producing moulds and infusoria. Cites Pouchet's demonstrations before the French Academy (1859) as supporting evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Force and substance are inseparable
rubrics_metrics.description: A body is the union of matter and form (substance); force and substance are inseparable and at bottom identical (e.g., matter as union of expansion and attraction).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because matter is the visibility of the will and every force is will, no force can appear without a material substratum and conversely no body can be without forces constituting its quality. Thus there is no opposition between force and substance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits of physics as ultimate explanation
rubrics_metrics.description: Physics cannot be placed on the throne of metaphysics because it leaves primary assumptions (e.g., inexplicable forces, vital force) untouched and therefore renounces the claim to provide ultimate explanations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Physics and physiology treat natural forces and vital force as given and are content to leave qualities as 'qualitates occultae.' The author argues that assuming 'indwelling forces' merely beggars ultimate understanding and turns explanations into incomprehensible miracles (see reference to chapter 17).

rubrics_metrics.name: Methodological starting-point of philosophy: subjectivity / self-consciousness
rubrics_metrics.description: Philosophy requires an absolutely immediate starting-point given in self-consciousness; the subjective (idea and will) is the proper foundation from which to proceed rather than the objective (matter assumed as thing-in-itself).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Author praises Descartes for starting from self-consciousness and argues that combining the two immediate data of idea and will allows a fuller philosophical development (analogy: two known quantities in algebra enable solving further). This is used as a critique of materialism, which illicitly assumes matter as absolute existence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Critique of materialism (petitio principii)
rubrics_metrics.description: Materialism's fundamental error is starting from the assumption that matter exists absolutely and unconditionally (independently of the knowing subject), which is a petitio principii and thus false.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If materialism were honest it would have to leave inherent qualities and forces unexplained as 'qualitates occultae' and treat physics/physiology as non-ultimate. This critique underpins the recommendation to begin philosophy from subjective immediate data rather than from an assumed objective matter.
